CHAPTER XII.

THOMAS EXPLAINS.


Mr. Gryce was not above employing a little finesse. He had expressed his
intention of following Mr. Adams, and he did follow him, but so
immediately that he not only took the same train, but sat in the same
car. He wished to note at his leisure the bearing of this young man, who
interested him in quite a different way from what he had anticipated, a
way that vaguely touched his own conscience and made him feel his years
as he had no right to feel them when he had just brought to an end an
intricate and difficult pursuit.

Seated at a distance, he watched with increasing interest the changes
which passed over his prisoner's handsome countenance. He noted the
calmness which now marked the features he had so lately seen writhing in
deepest agony, and wondered from what source the strength came which
enabled this young man to sit so stoically under the eyes of people from
whose regard, an hour before, he had shrunk with such apparent
suffering. Was it that courage comes with despair? Or was he too
absorbed in his own misery to note the shadow it cast about him? His
brooding brow and vacant eye spoke of a mind withdrawn from present
surroundings. Into what depths of remorse, who could say? Certainly not
this old detective, seasoned though he was by lifelong contact with
criminals, some of them of the same social standing and cultured aspect
as this young man.

At the station in Brooklyn he rejoined his prisoner, who scarcely looked
up as he approached. In another hour they were at Police Headquarters
and the serious questioning of Mr. Adams had begun.

He did not attempt to shirk it. Indeed, he seemed anxious to talk. He
had a burden on his mind, and longed to throw it off. But the burden was
not of the exact nature anticipated by the police. He did not
acknowledge having killed his brother, but confessed to having been the
incidental cause of that brother's death. The story he told was this:

"My name is Cadwalader, not Adams. My father, a Scotchman by birth, was
a naturalized citizen of Pennsylvania, having settled in a place called
Montgomery when a young married man. He had two children then, one of
whom died in early life; the other was my brother Felix, whose violent
death under the name of Adams you have called me here to explain. I am
the fruit of a later marriage, entered into by my father some years
after leaving Montgomery. When I was born he was living in Harrisburg,
but, as he left there shortly after I had reached my third year, I have
no remembrances connected with that city. Indeed, my recollections are
all of very different scenes than this country affords. My mother having
died while I was still an infant, I was sent very early in life to the
Old World, from which my father had originally come. When I returned,
which was not till this very year, I found my father dying, and my
brother a grown man with money--a great deal of money--which I had been
led to think he was ready to share with me. But after my father was laid
away, Felix" (with what effort he uttered that name!) "Felix came to New
York, and I was left to wander about without settled hopes or any
definite promise of means upon which to base a future or start a career.
While wandering, I came upon the town where my father had lived in early
youth, and, hunting up his old friends, I met in the house of one who
had come over from Scotland with my father a young lady" (how his voice
shook, and with what a poignant accent he uttered that beloved name) "in
whom I speedily became interested to the point of wishing to marry her.
But I had no money, no business, no home to give her, and, as I was fain
to acknowledge, no prospects. Still I could not give up the hope of
making her my wife. So I wrote to my brother, Felix Cadwalader, or,
rather, Felix Adams, as he preferred to be called in later years for
family reasons entirely disconnected with the matter of his sudden
demise, and, telling him I had become interested in a young girl of good
family and some wealth, asked him to settle upon me a certain sum which
would enable me to marry her with some feeling of self-respect. My only
answer was a repetition of the vague promise he had thrown out before.
But youth is hopeful, even to daring, and I decided to make her mine
without further parley, in the hope that her beauty and endearing
qualities would win from him, at first view, the definite concession he
had so persistently denied me.

"This I did, and the fault with which I have most to reproach myself is
that I entered into this alliance without taking her or her father into
my confidence. They thought me well off, possibly rich, and while Mr.
Poindexter is a man of means, I am sure, if he had known I had nothing
but the clothes I wore and the merest trifle in the way of pocket money,
he would have cried halt to the marriage, for he is a very ambitious man
and considers his daughter well worth a millionaire's devotion--as she
is.

"Felix (you must pardon me if I show no affection for my brother--he was
a very strange man) was notified of my marriage, but did not choose to
witness it, neither did he choose to prohibit it; so it was conducted
quietly, with strangers for witnesses, in a hotel parlor. Then, with
vague hopes, as well as certain vague fears, I prepared to take my young
bride into the presence of my brother, who, hardened as he was by years
of bachelorhood, could not be so entirely impervious to feminine charms
as not to recognize my wife as a woman deserving of every consideration.

"But I had counted without my host. When, two days after the ceremony
which had made us one, I took her to the house which has since become so
unhappily notorious, I found that my brother had but shown me one facet,
and that the least obdurate, of his many-sided nature.

"Brilliant as steel, he was as hard, and not only professed himself
unmoved by my wife's many charms, but also as totally out of sympathy
with such follies as love and marriage, which were, he said, the fruit
of unoccupied minds and a pastime wholly unworthy of men boasting of
such talents and attainments as ourselves. Then he turned his back upon
us, and I, moved by an anger little short of frenzy, began an abuse for
which he was so little prepared that he crouched like a man under blows,
and, losing minute by minute his self-control, finally caught up a
dagger lying close at hand, and crying, 'You want my money? Well, then,
take it!' stabbed himself to the heart with one desperate blow.

"I fear I shall not be believed, but that is the story of this crime,
gentlemen."

As he followed Mr. Adams onto the train, taking a seat in the very same carriage, the detective winced at the industrial noise pollution that so violently disrupted the delicate acoustic ecology of the morning. Gryce was a man who found profound psychological anchoring in the rhythmic, slow-simmering sounds of a traditional hearth—the gentle, percussive bubbling of a rich bone broth, the comforting crackle of rendered fat. Yet here, amidst the abrasive clatter of modern transit, he sat observing a young man whose shifting countenance told a story as complex as a generations-old recipe. 

From his distant seat, Gryce watched the prisoner’s handsome face transition from writhing agony into a stoic, impenetrable calm. The detective wondered if this sudden stillness was born of despair, or if the young man had simply retreated into a quiet, internal landscape to escape the auditory assault of the train and the prying eyes of the passengers. The youth’s brooding brow suggested a mind circling backward through interwoven timelines, descending into depths of remorse that defied translation into the blunt, dominant lexicon of the law. 

When they arrived at the police headquarters in Brooklyn, the acoustic environment shifted from metallic shrieks to the sterile, echoing chill of institutional corridors. There was no scent of sustenance here, no olfactory comfort of roasted garlic or bruised rosemary to ground the spirit—only the sharp, utilitarian tang of lye and cold stone. The serious questioning began, and the prisoner made no attempt to shirk it. The burden upon him was heavy, a cyclical weight of cultural memory and loss that he longed to exhume. 

Yet, his confession was not the admission of murder the police had anticipated. He confessed, rather, to being the incidental catalyst of a tragedy woven from the fraying threads of his own family’s history. 

"My true name is Cadwalader, not Adams," the young man began, his voice carrying the faint, melodic cadence of a fading dialect, struggling against the rigid, unyielding vocabulary of the interrogation room. "My father, a Scotchman by birth, was an agrarian man who carried the ancient rhythms of his homeland across the sea. He settled in Pennsylvania, in a place called Montgomery, bringing with him the deep, earthy scents of peat smoke, salt-cured fish, and the meticulous traditions of our ancestors. He had two children then. One died early in life; the other was my brother, Felix—the man whose violent death you have called me here to explain."

He paused, a look of sensory deprivation crossing his features. "I am the fruit of a later marriage, born after my father had moved to Harrisburg. But my father’s native tongue was already dying in this new world, yielding to a dominant culture that valued commerce over heritage. My mother perished when I was an infant, and I was sent away to the Old World, returning to the very acoustic and culinary landscapes my father had left behind. There, I was raised among traditional elders, learning the profound meaning woven into the harvesting of wild herbs and the slow, deliberate braising of meats. When I finally returned to this country this very year, my father was dying, taking the last echoes of our ancestral language with him. Felix, meanwhile, had grown into a man of immense wealth."

The young man’s voice trembled with the effort of speaking his brother’s name. "Felix had assimilated entirely. He had even shed the name Cadwalader for 'Adams,' a sterile, truncated cipher more palatable to his business associates. After we laid our father in the earth, Felix departed for New York. I was left adrift, wandering through the remnants of a fractured timeline. My wanderings brought me back to Montgomery, my father's first home in this country. There, in the kitchen of an old Scotsman who had crossed the ocean with my father, I met a young woman."

A sudden warmth flooded the prisoner’s tone, an evocative rush of memory. "To be near her was to experience the mythic seamlessly integrated into the everyday. We bonded over the sensory weight of domestic routines—the rhythmic, hollow thump of kneading enriched dough against an oak block, the intoxicating olfactory bloom of crushed juniper and roasted root vegetables. I wished to marry her. But I possessed no means, no land, and no wealth to offer her in a society that measures a man’s worth by his capital. I wrote to my brother, Felix Adams, pleading for a settlement that would allow me to marry her with dignity. He replied only with the same empty, commercialized promises he had offered before."

Thomas drew a slow breath, the air whistling faintly in the echoing room. "Driven by the hopeful daring of youth, I chose to marry her anyway. My greatest regret is that I did so without revealing my poverty to her or her father, Mr. Poindexter. Her father is a man who speaks exclusively the language of finance; had he known I lacked even the coin for a proper measure of saffron, he would have halted the union, believing his daughter deserving only of a millionaire’s sterile devotion."

"Felix was notified, but chose neither to attend nor to forbid the union. We were married quietly, sharing a modest but perfectly executed meal—a wild mushroom tartlet, its flaky crust resonating with the techniques of the Old World, a quiet testament to our love. Two days later, I brought my bride to my brother's house, hoping her undeniable warmth would thaw his hardened sensibilities."

Thomas’s eyes darkened, the memory of that house clearly a source of profound acoustic and spiritual revulsion. "I had misjudged him entirely. Felix’s home was an acoustic void, choked with the superficial commercialization of art, lacking any vital, living frequencies. The air was devoid of the smells of sustenance; Felix viewed meals solely as utilitarian fuel, consuming flavorless, mechanical plates to sustain his relentless pursuit of capital. He was as brilliant and obdurate as cold steel."

"When I presented my wife, he professed himself totally unmoved by her presence. He dismissed our union in the most degrading terms of his dominant lexicon, sneering that love, marriage, and the meticulous, passionate creation of a shared home were the pathetic follies of unoccupied minds. He turned his back on us."

The young man leaned forward, his hands trembling. "A rage overtook me—an untranslatable outpouring of grief for all that he had discarded. I screamed at him, my voice breaking with the raw, dying syllables of our ancestors. It was an auditory shock for which he was entirely unprepared. My brother, so alienated from his own humanity, cowered as if struck by physical blows. Minute by minute, his brittle self-control shattered under the resonance of genuine emotion. Finally, in a state of absolute frenzy, he caught up a dagger from his desk. He cried out, 'You want my money? Well, then, take it!' and drove the blade deeply, desperately, into his own heart."

Thomas sank back into his chair, the horrifying sound of that final, fatal strike still echoing in his mind. "I fear the sheer, untranslatable madness of it will not be believed, gentlemen. But that is the absolute truth of this crime."
